article_text:
In the summer of 1983, Cyndi Lauper arrived at Coney Island in New York with Annie Leibovitz to shoot the cover of her debut album She’s So Unusual . Decked out in a red vintage dress, dripping with costume jewelry, and sporting a head of flaming orange hair, Lauper posed outside an old wax museum. Standing against its graffitied facade, a thought came to her: “In the darkest place, shed the brightest light,” she wrote in her 2012 memoir .

Some of Lauper’s brightest colors are now resurfacing more than 40 years after she first blazed a trail across pop music. In two sales at Bonhams in New York later this month, the icon is offloading dozens of stage-worn outfits that helped define her career, in addition to instruments, memorabilia, props, and personal artifacts. For the “Time After Time” singer, now 73, bringing these singular, offbeat ensembles together evokes “a time when things were run by creatives,” she told me.

Cyndi Lauper in concert in France, 1994. Photo: Alain Benainous / Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images.

“Everything has become corporate and creatives are being squashed out because we are all supposed to have braces on our brains and not be individualistic anymore,” she said over a video call. “I thought it would be good to remind people of when fashion and rock ‘n’ roll merged, when we did wild things.”

The wild things crossing the auction block include the red plaid dress that Lauper wore to the inaugural MTV Video Music Awards in 1984 (estimate: $800–$1,200); the leopard-print pajamas seen in the “ Girls Just Want to Have Fun ” music video ($500–$700); and the metal bra from the “ True Colors ” music video ($1,000–$1,500).

Leopard print pajamas from the “Girls Just Want to Have Fun” music video (1983). Photo courtesy of Bonhams.

There are designer pieces by Vivienne Westwood and Alexander McQueen , as well as vintage items from Screaming Mimi’s , the boutique where Lauper worked before she attained pop stardom.

Some others are unique creations, like the newly restored newspaper skirt ensemble that Lauper wore on the cover of 1986’s True Colors ($1,000–$2,000). Laura Wills , founder of Screaming Mimi’s, made the piece by stapling strips of newspaper onto a hoop skirt. Lauper spray-painted a pair of shoes to match. “I spray-painted a lot of shit,” she said.

Newspaper skirt ensemble from the True Colors (1986) album cover shoot. Photo courtesy of Bonhams.

“For her, every single outfit, every single look was part of the music, part of the whole inspiration,” Anna Hicks , Bonhams’s head of private and iconic collections, told me. “Everything she wore and everything she did was extremely intentional, even though it just looks so fun and crazy.”

Lauper’s looks in the 1980s though the ‘90s have been endlessly imitated but never surpassed. Born in Brooklyn, she grew up with grandparents who worked in the fashion industry, and honed her style education at Screaming Mimi’s, where she and Wills plotted maximalist looks. Fingerless gloves, oversized jackets, rhinestone chains, prom dresses, lace scarves—all were matched and mingled. A one-time art major at Johnson State College in Vermont (“Don’t ask me why I’ve never continued”), she approached fashion with an artist’s flair and a rebel’s instincts.

Cyndi Lauper. Photo: Greyshock, courtesy of Bonhams.

In our conversation, Lauper described hair as “sculpture” and a turquoise Dolce & Gabbana derby she’d customized with feathers as a “twisted Magritte .” She recalled wearing late stylist Biff Chandler ’s painted corsets as blouses in the 1980s as a way to counter their confining form and legacy.

But above all is Lauper’s love for color. Her outfits popped with the boldest reds, greens, and pinks, and her hair was never without an electric hue. “If you’re gonna wear a circle skirt, you could put another crinoline under that. So if you spun across the stage, you’re looking at splashes of color,” she said. Not surprisingly, she named Jackson Pollock as a big influence.

“That was inspiration, using color that would explode,” she said. “You could wear it, you could dance on it, you could live in it. You know, living art.”

Cyndi Lauper at the Limelight nightclub in New York, 1984. Photo: Vinnie Zuffante / Getty Images.

For the video for her 1984 cover of “ Money Changes Everything ,” Lauper created a large splatter painting that was used as the floor of the set. She appears in a white fringe vest, a jacket turned inside-out, and mismatched shoes, dancing and kicking a trash can across a stage. “I couldn’t afford a cherry picker, so they gave me the garbage can,” she said. She called the whole thing “moving art.”

Lauper’s scrappy, punky aesthetic has made her a beacon of unfiltered self-expression, a spirit she has also channeled into her Broadway work and LGBTQ+ advocacy. She remains fabulously turned-out. The Bonhams auction offers some of her recent fashion outings, such as the bejeweled McQueen cape she donned at the 2014 Grammy Awards ($1,200–$1,800) and most outrageously, the towering rainbow headdress she wore as grand marshal of the 2003 West Hollywood Pride Parade ($600–$800). There’s even a new assemblage she created around a pair of hand-painted pumps ($1,000–$1,500).

Rainbow headdress and rainbow dress Cyndi Lauper wore as Grand Marshal of the 2003 West Hollywood Pride Parade. Photo courtesy of Bonhams.

When she was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame last year, Lauper arrived in a crystal-encrusted suit with a shock of seafoam-colored hair. She was honored by pop singer Chappell Roan , who, wearing a replica of the newspaper skirt , called Lauper the “woman who redefined what a pop star could look like, sound like, sing like, and be.” Now, as her collection heads to auction, Lauper hopes to inspire a few more rule-breakers.

“It’s so amazing the things you do that you struggle to get through the gatekeepers,” she said. “And actually, the kids heard it. Some little kid was watching, going, ‘I love that.’”

Cyndi Lauper: Suitcase of Memories, Part I is a live auction at Bonhams New York on October 22. Part II runs online through October 23.

article_text:
Il punto d’inizio è sempre un incontro, una conversazione. Una cena che si prolunga, una storia raccontata tra una portata e l’altra, una parola di troppo capace di accendere un’idea. È da questa immagine, semplice e profondamente quotidiana, che prende forma il mondo di Hartis, la maison francese di arredi contemporanei da collezione fondata nel 2021 da Hugo Besnier. Prima ancora di disegnare un mobile, Besnier sembra porsi una domanda essenziale: che cosa rende piacevole il tempo trascorso insieme? La risposta prende forma questo autunno a Parigi, in un loft storico della Cour de Rohan, nel cuore di Saint-Germain-des-Prés, che ha inaugurato durante la Paris Art Week (durante la settimana densa e vorticosa di Art Basel Paris ) ma è in programma su appuntamento fino al 30 novembre. È qui che Hartis presenta le nuove creazioni della collezione Tour de Mains, in un ambiente in cui arredi, opere d’arte e ceramiche dialogano attraverso affinità estetiche e sensibilità condivise.

Il design, prima di tutto, è fatto per essere vissuto

Le novità ampliano il vocabolario di Tour de Mains e presentano oggetti speciali come la testiera Biseau, i comodini Atelier e le lampade da tavolo Pointe, affiancati dai tavolini da caffè Grains, dalla panca Hache e dalle applique Maillon e Fusion. Ma oltre al prodotto, c’è molto di più: il filo conduttore è una concezione dell’arredo che mette al centro il corpo, il comfort e la relazione tra le persone. Le forme, le proporzioni e la scelta dei materiali non rispondono soltanto a un’esigenza estetica, sono pensate per accogliere i gesti quotidiani, dal sedersi a tavola all’appoggiare una tazza su un tavolino, senza interrompere il piacere di una conversazione.

«Amo il buon cibo e amo ricevere», racconta Hugo Besnier. Quando progetta un mobile, spiega, pensa innanzitutto al comfort che saprà offrire al corpo e alle conversazioni che potrà ospitare. Bordi arrotondati, una seduta morbida, un tavolo da pranzo con la profondità giusta: ogni dettaglio contribuisce a creare le condizioni per restare a tavola per ore, senza fretta. È una visione del design che rifugge l’idea dell’oggetto come semplice presenza scenografica. I mobili diventano piuttosto presenze discrete, capaci di accompagnare la vita e favorire la convivialità. Non semplici oggetti, ma oggetti di conversazione.

Un loft parigino, tra arte e memoria

A dare forma a questo universo è l’interior design di Hugo Besnier, che costruisce un insieme di arredi, ceramiche e opere d’arte selezionate secondo affinità personali. Con il supporto di Hervé Mikaeloff, sulle pareti del loft trovano posto lavori di Balthus, Judit Reigl, David Hockney, Sheila Hicks, André Masson, Pablo Picasso, Setsuko, Alberto Giacometti e Henri Michaux. La scelta degli artisti si lega anche alla storia della Cour de Rohan, luogo che dalla fine dell’Ottocento ospita artisti e atelier. E si sposa senza attrito con gli arredi della collezione Tour de Mains, condividendo lo stesso spazio, e arricchendolo, senza perdere la propria identità. Visitando il loft, la prima idea è quella di una raccolta personale, realizzata secondo un’unico sguardo e un’unica sensibilità.

La materia, il gesto, il tempo

Fondata nel 2021, Hartis è una maison francese specializzata in arredi contemporanei da collezione. La collezione Tour de Mains nasce da una ricerca paziente sulla convivialità, sostenuta da una particolare attenzione alla manifattura. Legno, pelle, pietra e vetro vengono lavorati da artigiani selezionati, attraverso gesti che comprendono l’assemblaggio, la regolazione e la lucidatura. È proprio in questo rapporto tra materia e lavoro manuale che si riconosce un altro aspetto della filosofia di Besnier: ogni oggetto deve essere curato tanto nella sua realizzazione quanto nell’esperienza che offrirà a chi lo utilizzerà. La precisione artigianale non è fine a se stessa, ma contribuisce a definire la qualità del contatto, la comodità di una seduta, la naturalezza di un gesto. I mobili invitano a fermarsi, e il lusso smette di esaurirsi nell’oggetto, per prendere forma nella sua condivisione.

"“第一次看这部电影时，甚至是在纽约，因为虽然我当时离得不远且参与了前期制作，但我并没有去片场。他们去的很多地方都是我曾经成长、甚至真正生活过的地方。所以我不知道自己在那些时刻坐在片场会有什么感觉。但我确实记得在银幕上、在放映室里看过其中的绝大部分片段，它们非常美丽。我当时首先想到的是：‘哇，我太高兴这个作品存在了。我太高兴这些记忆能以这种方式被永垂不朽，由这些杰出的艺术家将它们呈现出来，让我们所有人都能看到。’", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“在多伦多国际电影节（TIFF）观看时，发生了点别的事情，那就是：‘哦，哇。现在我要和2,200人一起分享所有这些东西了。’我完全没想到。我得告诉你们，我也和很多人说过，不管别人觉得这有多天真或目光短浅，我当时真的觉得：‘好吧，总共大概也就几万或几十万人会看这部电影吧。’我是看着独立电影长大的。我在迈阿密长大，经常去O Cinema之类的地方，我的导师总是带我们去这里的电影院看艺术片。所以哪怕当时这里在拍摄《绝地战警》这样的大片，我们依然在看《夜幕降临前》，我们对这种模式已经习以为常了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“所以我对那种体量很习惯，觉得：‘这将会是对那种传统的一个很好的补充。’然而看到它超越了那个范畴、正在突破界限，看到可能会有数百万人看到这部电影，这彻底震撼了我的世界。我不知道自己是否已经完全接受了这件事。这就是为什么直到现在，当别人想跟我聊这部电影时，我看起来还是会感到震惊和意外。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": 埃弗雷特收藏馆供图", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "谈马赫沙拉·阿里在《月光男孩》中赢得奥斯卡奖的胡安（Juan）一角", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“马赫沙拉和我曾在《月光男孩》之前就有过交集，因为他本该出演我的话剧《红水与褐水》（In the Red and Brown Water）。他是一位出色的演员，当时就在舞台上演出，我们当时正试图让他加入这部剧，他给我留了便条，说非常抱歉他得去演另一部话剧，所以我们没能合作成。因此我们最后没能在那个项目上合作，但我非常欣赏他的作品，也很喜欢他在舞台和电视上的表现。当时，他正在拍摄两到三部剧。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“所以，当巴里说‘嘿，这就是我们打算找来演胡安的人’时，我说：‘行，那就他吧。’我一直觉得这在情理之中，而且这个角色显然是以某个对我年轻时的人生产生过深远影响的人为原型的。所以我毫不怀疑马赫沙拉会表现得非凡卓越。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "谈娜奥米·哈里斯在《月光男孩》中获得奥斯卡提名的宝拉（Paula）一角", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“这太不可思议了。她大约只有三四天的时间在片场拍摄所有这些戏。我以前并不认识娜奥米，但她是一位杰出的艺术家，一上场就直接进入状态，看着极其震撼。有时甚至很难看下去，因为她进入的那种状态——那个角色简直跟她本人没有半点相似之处。特别是在前半部分，她真正体现了我母亲身上的很多特质，接着是她在电影中逐渐走向颓废、经历我母亲曾经历过的某种恐惧。谢天谢地，巴里保留了剧本中电影里出现的那场和解戏。他保留了这一段，并且在此基础上以一种非常华丽、非常美丽的方式进行了构建。所以我对她的演绎、对她敢于触碰那个深度永远心怀感激，因为她本可以选择稳妥的演法，但她没有。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "谈《月光男孩》的视觉遗产", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当时，在我们制作并首映这部电影时，大众化民主化的创作、或是人们进行电影或视觉表达的能力已经迎来了爆发。事实上，我后来拍的下一部电影就是用iPhone拍摄的。因此，人们进行视觉表达并走向电影成功的可能性变得更加切实、更加触手可及。有很多人当时都在想：‘嗯，既然那些人能做到这一点，那我也可以这样做。’这真的非常非凡。我有无数人给我写信说：‘这让我去读了电影学院。这让我以某种方式开始接触摄影。这让我成为了一名摄影师。’真的，我有好多朋友都说：‘对啊，我写作，但现在我同时也是一名摄影师，我对此非常认真，我真的很关注视觉镜头。’所以这太了不起了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“这种影响，对我来说很大程度上在于能够说：‘嘿，我需要拍这部电影，因为我需要看到我自己，或者至少看到我以前没有看到的自己身上的某些部分。’我想很多人都觉得：‘是的，我也需要这样做。’对此我心怀感激。这种情况确实会发生：电影会适时出现并做到这一点。电影会出现，或者歌曲会出现，或者艺术中会发生某种事情，让人们觉得：‘哦，那个艺术家真的很需要看到那样对他们自身的描绘。我也感同身受，也想这样做。’所以再次重申，这对其他人来说正在发生，对我而言也是一份厚礼。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当你想到对黑人群体、尤其是黑人酷儿群体的描绘时，这部电影拥有某种程度的亲密感，让人们意识到：‘哦，哇，在这样一个平时不常被看到的题材上，你竟然可以做到如此脆弱。’再次说明，当我提到脆弱时，我指的是镜头的紧凑度、以及我们以前从未见我们在大银幕上窥视得如此深邃的眼神。我们在无数电影中都拍过特写。如果你回过头去看看某些黑色电影（noir），你能看到铺天盖地的关于X、Y、Z的特写，但当你观看像《普通人》（Ordinary People）这样的作品时，你会发现摄影机能够贴得多么近、多么亲密，深入到那种炙热之中。当然也有一些仪式的例子，比如胡安为Chiron/Little施洗，但这类例子屈指可数、少之又少。这部电影在说：‘嘿，你可以更贴近这些，可以做更多这样的尝试。’很多电影制作人通过这种方式找到了他们的美学理念、找到了他们的切入点，并留下了他们自己独特的印记，这真是非凡之举。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/P1143WVW.jpg?w=650", "alt": "Barry Jenkins and Tarell Alvin McCraney - Writing (Adapted Screenplay) - 'Moonlight'", "caption": "巴里·詹金斯与塔勒尔·阿尔文·麦卡尼 —— 最佳改编剧本 —— 《月光男孩》 Stephen Lovekin/WWD/PMC", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "关于《月光男孩》入围最佳改编剧本奖类别 —— 尽管该戏剧从未被搬上舞台", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“《藩篱》是一部戏剧，后来被改编成电影，所以归入改编类是说得通的。话说回来，你把一部短片变成长片，这本身也是一种改编。所以觉得在这个类别里很合适，那是肯定的。巴里确实把它真正拍成了一部长片。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“最初的剧本以一种非常循环的方式讲述这个故事，意思是你会醒来，然后发现你同时看到了 Little、Chiron 和 Black 一整天的生活。所以你会看到其中一个人醒来洗脸，另一个人起身洗脸。在某个时刻，你会意识到你看到的是同一个人的生命。巴里觉得，‘不，我们可以把它分成章节，让它更线性一些。’ ”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“然后，他当然对电影最后20到30分钟进行了颠覆。［这］体现了巴里·詹金斯极为精彩的切入方式，同时又塞进了很多我在自己生活中会做的琐事。当时我就想，‘你是怎么做到的……’所以是的，这绝对是改编。能与他在那方面合作真是不可思议，我希望我们能有更多这样的合作机会。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "关于《月光男孩》是否与《爱乐之城》的最佳影片乌龙事件过于纠缠不清", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“这是那种‘事情就是这样’的情况。就像故事里那样，胡安从 Little 的生活中消失了，这也是那些顺其自然、本该如此的事情之一。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“而且我不认为这在任何方面玷污了这部电影。电影依然是那部电影。但好吧，事情确实发生了，无论它以何种方式显现，我都心怀感激。我无法撤销它。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我记得曾对我的朋友杰瑞米·波普说过这样的话 —— 不仅仅是谈论这件事，而是谈论整个人生 —— 我说：‘杰伊，如果你不把这一切都视为喜悦，那你就会没完没了地数落个不停。’你必须把这一切都当成喜悦。每一次你都得把这一切看作喜悦，这感觉就像是那种值得感恩的时刻。你只要把我们正朝着这个方向前进、我们迎来了第10个年头、以及这部由许多伟大的人投入了难以置信的心血的电影在许多方面得到认可，统统视为一种喜悦。”", "links": [{"text": "Jeremy Pope", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/awards/consider-this/jeremy-pope-the-inspection-interview-1234784648/"}], "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "The word playwright and screenwriter Tarell Alvin McCraney uses to describe his thoughts on the journey his deeply personal film “ Moonlight ” continues to have is “incredible.” Wednesday, October 21, marks 10 years since the Best Picture Oscar winner was released to the masses. ”Seeing it now is worth the price of admission,” said the Best Adapted Screenplay Oscar winner to IndieWire over Zoom.", "links": [{"text": "Tarell Alvin McCraney", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/tarell-alvin-mccraney/"}, {"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}, {"text": "Moonlight", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/moonlight/"}, {"text": "Best Picture Oscar winner", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/awards/industry/moonlight-wins-oscar-best-picture-academy-awards-1201787590/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "An adaptation of his unproduced play “In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue,” written with director Barry Jenkins , “Moonlight” still has McCraney asking himself the fundamental question, “‘Who am I and who can I be?’ And that’s powerful.”", "links": [{"text": "Barry Jenkins", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/barry-jenkins-moonlight-best-movie-decade-1202159932/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screen-Shot-2026-09-07-at-5.18.25-PM.png?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "'Musk'", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/PatrickStewartObituary.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "patrick stewart obituary", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The current Geffen Playhouse artistic director, who is still working on many TV and film projects he is not yet allowed to discuss, said, “I’m still expanding like the universe. And the moment that I stop, the moment that I just sit in it, then where am I?”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Read on for more of McCraney reflecting on “Moonlight” at 10 below."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "How “Moonlight” Came to Be"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“So ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ was a film, a screenplay that I wrote in 2003, right after the death of my mother. She died of AIDS-related complications. And I had written a play called ‘The Brothers Size’ for my entry into the Yale School of Drama and the script called ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue.’ I had written both of them because, one, I was making an application for grad school, but two, my teacher, Rafael Lima, who was our playwriting and screenplay teacher in high school, always told me that if a story was coming to you visually, then it’s a film. If you heard it, it was a play. So ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ was always slated to be a film because it was coming to me in images, but I’d written it in a kind of hybrid, what I call a medium length."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“It wasn’t a full feature at the time. I previously had written a short in high school called ‘Silent Type,’ and it was more about me trying to put down the memories I was having of growing up in Liberty City. Now, I understand it’s something most people do when losing a parent. They sort of start trying to recollect their earliest memories and put them back together again. So that’s how ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ came about. But in 2003, an indie film about a gay kid in Miami was probably a hard feat, especially for a just-recently-graduated undergrad. So André Holland , who I met later, had read a copy of it, Glenn Davis, who runs Steppenwolf, we had all read a copy and tried to make it into a film in Chicago. Then I quickly sort of said, ‘No, this is where we stay.’ And it stayed in my computer for probably another 10 years until I met Barry Jenkins in around 2012, 2013.", "links": [{"text": "André Holland", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/interviews/andre-holland-moonlight-legacy-the-knick-season-3-interview-1235148134/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We were both making a film in a film festival here in Miami. We had a couple meetings, and found out we grew up blocks away from each other. Barry said, ‘Look, I want to make this into a film. I’ve read the script.’ Our friend Andrew Hevia had given it to him. He said, ‘I think I can make this into a full feature.’ I was like, ‘Great, we should.’ He didn’t believe me a few times. This is before there was an A24 or Plan B involved. So I think he thought I didn’t believe him. He kept going back, getting more support, and saying, ‘Look, we’re going to make this into a film.’ I kept going, ‘Yes, yes you are.’", "links": [{"text": "A24", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/a24/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“So even to this day, he said, ‘Yeah, you did have to say yes to me a few times before I believed you.’ But yeah, that’s how we came together on the film. Barry did an incredible job of turning it into a full feature, taking the story that was already there and taking it from a place of memory into a place of palpability and something that we all could feel.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/635334852.jpg?w=650", "alt": "Oscar-nominated director Barry Jenkins and Playwright Tarell Alvin McCraney take part in a Q+A after a preview screening of Moonlight at BFI Southbank on February 14, 2017 in London, United Kingdom.", "caption": "Oscar-nominated director Barry Jenkins and Playwright Tarell Alvin McCraney take part in a Q+A after a preview screening of Moonlight at BFI Southbank on February 14, 2017, in London, United Kingdom. You should know each other.’"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“YoungArts was instrumental in giving us space to do pre-production for ‘Moonlight.’ That organization has really carved a path for arts in this community in a way that national foundations rarely do. So I’m ever grateful for them and wish them nothing but success and hope that other national organizations, that the government, that our local folks really help celebrate them and keep them around for a long time.”"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "On How He Saw “Moonlight” for the First Time"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Watching it for the first time, even in New York, because though I was near and helping on production, I was not on set. But I do remember watching a great deal of those moments on film, in screening rooms, and it was beautiful. First I thought, ‘Wow, I’m so glad that this exists. I’m so glad that these memories have been immortalized in these ways with these incredible artists rendering it for all of us to see.’"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Seeing it at TIFF, something else happened, which was like, ‘Oh, wow. I will tell you, and I’ve said to many people, whether people think it’s naïve or shortsighted, I really thought, ‘Yeah, a few hundred thousand people may see this film in total.’ I grew up on indie films. article_text:
The word playwright and screenwriter Tarell Alvin McCraney uses to describe his thoughts on the journey his deeply personal film “ Moonlight ” continues to have is “incredible.” Wednesday, October 21, marks 10 years since the Best Picture Oscar winner was released to the masses. ”Seeing it now is worth the price of admission,” said the Best Adapted Screenplay Oscar winner to IndieWire over Zoom.

An adaptation of his unproduced play “In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue,” written with director Barry Jenkins , “Moonlight” still has McCraney asking himself the fundamental question, “‘Who am I and who can I be?’ And that’s powerful.”

The current Geffen Playhouse artistic director, who is still working on many TV and film projects he is not yet allowed to discuss, said, “I’m still expanding like the universe. And the moment that I stop, the moment that I just sit in it, then where am I?”

Read on for more of McCraney reflecting on “Moonlight” at 10 below.

How “Moonlight” Came to Be

“So ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ was a film, a screenplay that I wrote in 2003, right after the death of my mother. She died of AIDS-related complications. And I had written a play called ‘The Brothers Size’ for my entry into the Yale School of Drama and the script called ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue.’ I had written both of them because, one, I was making an application for grad school, but two, my teacher, Rafael Lima, who was our playwriting and screenplay teacher in high school, always told me that if a story was coming to you visually, then it’s a film. If you heard it, it was a play. So ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ was always slated to be a film because it was coming to me in images, but I’d written it in a kind of hybrid, what I call a medium length.

“It wasn’t a full feature at the time. I previously had written a short in high school called ‘Silent Type,’ and it was more about me trying to put down the memories I was having of growing up in Liberty City. Now, I understand it’s something most people do when losing a parent. They sort of start trying to recollect their earliest memories and put them back together again. So that’s how ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ came about. But in 2003, an indie film about a gay kid in Miami was probably a hard feat, especially for a just-recently-graduated undergrad. So André Holland , who I met later, had read a copy of it, Glenn Davis, who runs Steppenwolf, we had all read a copy and tried to make it into a film in Chicago. Then I quickly sort of said, ‘No, this is where we stay.’ And it stayed in my computer for probably another 10 years until I met Barry Jenkins in around 2012, 2013.

“We were both making a film in a film festival here in Miami. We had a couple meetings, and found out we grew up blocks away from each other. Barry said, ‘Look, I want to make this into a film. I’ve read the script.’ Our friend Andrew Hevia had given it to him. He said, ‘I think I can make this into a full feature.’ I was like, ‘Great, we should.’ He didn’t believe me a few times. This is before there was an A24 or Plan B involved. So I think he thought I didn’t believe him. He kept going back, getting more support, and saying, ‘Look, we’re going to make this into a film.’ I kept going, ‘Yes, yes you are.’

“So even to this day, he said, ‘Yeah, you did have to say yes to me a few times before I believed you.’ But yeah, that’s how we came together on the film. Barry did an incredible job of turning it into a full feature, taking the story that was already there and taking it from a place of memory into a place of palpability and something that we all could feel.”

On the Role YoungArts Played in “Moonlight” Being Made

“I have had an incredible education in art thanks to Miami. Miami’s art has been nurtured in a real way by YoungArts, specifically young artists, because it brings in artists from all over the world.

“I remember sneaking out of playwriting class to go to YoungArts to see the YoungArts finalists and thinking, ‘Those dancers are doing what I’m supposed to be doing in their form right now. Their dedication, their ability to control their body and use their technique is — ’ And I’m just over here in this acting class trying to remember my lines. I just thought even then, ‘I’ve got to get my shit together.’

“And so YoungArts has really paved a way for that. They have really dedicated themselves to nurturing the local artists, but also bringing in young artists and supporting them for longer stretches of time. That’s been so helpful. Andrew Hevia, who was an arts finalist, is the reason why Barry Jenkins and I met each other because he was producing films and said to us, ‘Hey, you both are Miami. You both have Miami connections. You should know each other.’

“YoungArts was instrumental in giving us space to do pre-production for ‘Moonlight.’ That organization has really carved a path for arts in this community in a way that national foundations rarely do. So I’m ever grateful for them and wish them nothing but success and hope that other national organizations, that the government, that our local folks really help celebrate them and keep them around for a long time.”

On How He Saw “Moonlight” for the First Time

“Watching it for the first time, even in New York, because though I was near and helping on production, I was not on set. There were just too many places that they were going to that were places I had grown up and places that I had actually lived in. So I didn’t know how I would feel sitting on a set in those moments. But I do remember watching a great deal of those moments on film, in screening rooms, and it was beautiful. First I thought, ‘Wow, I’m so glad that this exists. I’m so glad that these memories have been immortalized in these ways with these incredible artists rendering it for all of us to see.’

“Seeing it at TIFF, something else happened, which was like, ‘Oh, wow. And now I’m sharing all of these things with 2,200 people.’ And I did not expect that. I will tell you, and I’ve said to many people, whether people think it’s naïve or shortsighted, I really thought, ‘Yeah, a few hundred thousand people may see this film in total.’ I grew up on indie films. I grew up in Miami going to places like O Cinema, and my mentor would take us to art films all the time here in the cinema. So it was something that we were used to even when the blockbusters like ‘Bad Boys’ were being made here, we were still watching ‘Before Night Falls.’

“So I was used to that and thought, ‘This is going to be a great addition to that.’ It blew my mind to see that it was going beyond that, that it was pushing past that, that this was going to be seen by maybe millions of people. I don’t know that I’ve still come to full terms with that. It’s the reason why I look shocked and surprised when people want to talk to me about the film even now.”

On Mahershala Ali’s Oscar-Winning Performance as Juan in “Moonlight”

“Mahershala and I crossed paths prior to ‘Moonlight’ because he was supposed to be in my play ‘In the Red and Brown Water.’ He is an incredible actor and was on stage then, and we were trying to get him into this play, and he sent me this note saying he’s so sorry he had to go do this other play and we couldn’t do it. So we ended up not working together on that, but I admired his work and loved seeing him on stage and on television as well. At the time, he was filming two or three shows.

“So when it came to the moment where Barry said, ‘Hey, here’s who we’re going to for Juan,’ I said, ‘Yeah, that’ll do.’ I always felt like it made sense, and the character clearly is based on someone who made a deep influence on my life as a young person. So there was no doubt in my mind that Mahershala would be extraordinary.”

On Naomie Harris’ Oscar-Nominated Performance as Paula in “Moonlight”

“It was incredible. She had about three or four days on set to film all of that. I didn’t know Naomie before, but she is an incredible artist who came in and just went , and it was extraordinary to watch. Sometimes it was hard to watch because she just went to this place where — that character couldn’t be more not like her. And especially in the earlier moments where she really embodies a lot of what my mother stood for, and then in the decline that she has in the film, some of the terror that my mother was going through. Thankfully, Barry kept the reconciliation that happens in the film that was in the script. He kept that and actually built on it in a way that was really gorgeous and really beautiful. So I was ever grateful for her portrayal, for going there, because she could have played it safe and she didn’t.”

On the Visual Legacy of “Moonlight”

“At the time, when we were both making and premiering the film, the democratizing, or the ability for folks to make film or visual depictions has exploded. In fact, the next film that I did make was shot on an iPhone. So the ability for people to make visual depictions and reach towards cinematic success became more palpable or more accessible. There were a lot of folks who were going, ‘Well, if those folks can do that, I can do this.’ And that was really extraordinary. I had tons of people write and say, ‘This made me go to film school. This made me take up cinematography in a way. This made me become a photographer.’ Literally, I have so many friends who just went, ‘Yeah, I write, but now I’m also a photographer, and I take it seriously, and I’m really about visual lenses.’ So that’s been extraordinary.

“That impact, a lot of it for me was being able to say, ‘Hey, I needed to make this film because I needed to see myself, or at least parts of myself that I wasn’t seeing.’ And I think a lot of folks went, ‘Yeah, I need to do the same.’ And I am grateful for that. And that happens: Films come along and do that. Films come along, or songs come along, or something happens in art where people go, ‘Oh, that artist really needed to see that depiction of themselves. I feel that, too, and want to do the same.’ So again, it was a gift to me that it is happening for other folks.

“When you think of a depiction of Black folk, specifically Black queer folks, there is a level of intimacy that the film has that folks recognized as ‘Oh wow, you can get that vulnerable on a subject that isn’t often seen.’ And again, when I say vulnerable, I mean the closeness of the shots, the deep peering into eyes that we hadn’t seen before. We’ve done that on tons of film. If you go back and look at some of the noir, you can get tons of close-ups of X, Y, and Z, but you watch things like ‘Ordinary People,’ and you see just how close and intimate, into the heat, that the camera gets. There are, of course, examples of those rituals like the baptism that happens to Chiron/Little by Juan, but they’re fewer and far between. The film is saying, ‘Hey, you can get closer to this and do more of it.’ And there’s a lot of filmmakers who have found their ideology, their way in through that, and found their own unique stamp to put on it, which is extraordinary.”

On “Moonlight” Entering the Best Adapted Screenplay Category — Even Though the Play Was Never Produced

“‘Fences’ is a play and then was adapted into a film, and so Adapted made sense. Again, you take a short, and you turn it into a feature length, and that’s an adaptation too. So it felt right to be there, for sure. Barry did really make it into a feature.

“The original script told this story in a very circular way, meaning you woke up and you realized that you would see the day going on of Little, Chiron, and Black all at once. So you would see one wake up, wash their face, the other get up, wash their face. At some point you realized that this was one life that you were watching. Barry thought, ‘No, we can chapter this out and make this more linear.’

“And then, he, of course, blew up that last 20 to 30 minutes of the film. [It] is an incredible Barry Jenkins lean-in, but peppering tons of shit that I do in my own life. I was like, ‘How did you…’ So yeah, adaptation, absolutely. It was incredible to collaborate with him on that, and I wish we could do it more.”

On Whether “Moonlight” Is Too Enmeshed with the Best Picture Mix-Up with “La La Land”

“It’s one of those things that just is . It’s like in the story, Juan disappears out of Little’s life, and it is just one of those things that is.

“And I don’t think that has tarnished the film in any way. The film is still the film. But yeah, it happened, and I’m grateful for however it manifested. I can’t undo it.

“I remember saying this to my friend Jeremy Pope — not just talking about this, but just life in general — I said, ‘Jay, if you don’t count it all joy, then you won’t stop counting.’ You have to count it all as joy. Every time you have to count it all joy, and it feels like one of those counts. You just count it all joy that we are headed towards this direction, that we’re 10 years out, and that this film that a lot of wonderful people put a lot of incredible work into was recognized in many ways.”
excerpt_original: The Oscar-winning screenwriter reflects on the beginnings of Barry Jenkins' "Moonlight" — and how it led to multiple Academy Awards, including Best Picture.

article_text:
Announcement

Discover Marcel Duchamp at the Philadelphia Museum of Art

See 300+ unique works by Marcel Duchamp, including the permanently installed masterpiece “Étant donnés”, exclusively at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

Duchamp's practice was one of continuous self-reinvention, impossible to categorize under any label.

In 1912, the artist Marcel Duchamp (1887-1968) began to question his occupation. He decided at the age of twenty-five to abandon the craft of oil painting. He also strove to make himself aloof from the art world to work as he pleased. Duchamp went on to become one of the most innovative and original figures in the history of modern art. Across six decades, he was associated with Cubism, Dada, and Surrealism.

The first major U.S. retrospective dedicated to Marcel Duchamp in more than 50 years, this exhibition will explore the range and arc of this artist’s illustrious career. Marcel Duchamp will feature a chronological display of more than 300 works of painting, sculpture, film, photography, printed matter, exhibition design, and the unclassifiable works known as readymades. It will present Duchamp's most renowned creations, including the provocative "Nude Descending a Staircase (No. 2)" (1912); his magnum opus, "The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even" (1915-23); the iconoclastic "Fountain" (1917) and "L.H.O.O.Q." (1919); "Box in a Valise" (1935-41), the artist’s portable museum of his own creations in miniature; and "Étant donnés" (1946-66), Duchamp’s final major work in which he reflected upon his lifelong artistic obsessions.

Plan your visit today and discover Marcel Duchamp at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

Learn more and buy tickets at philamuseum.org .

article_text:
EMBODIED is space for photographers exploring body politics, embodiment, identity, and lived experience.

We are looking for photographers whose work explores the body as a site of politics, experience, or identity, and work rooted in personal or collective lived experience, across any medium and from any geography. Selected submissions are featured on our Instagram and shared with our growing community.

Until December 31st

Apply here

article_text:
トラック運転手が畑で発見、古代ローマの金の指輪が博物館へ──発見者は住宅ローン完済｜イングランド南西部サマセット州の農地で金属探知機愛好家が発見したローマ時代の金の指輪が、地元の遺産保護団体に購入され、サマセット博物館で展示されることになった。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy South West Heritage Trust

イルミンスター近郊の農地で見つかったイルミンスター・リング。Photo: Courtesy South West Heritage Trust

英金属探知機愛好家、有機農場で古代ローマの鉛インゴットを発見。帝国時代の鉱物供給網のヒントに｜イギリス・ウェールズのセレディギオン州で、金属探知機愛好家の2人が古代ローマ時代の鉛インゴット2点を発見した。皇帝ドミティアヌスの刻印が残るこれらの遺物は、この地域がローマ帝国の資源供給網に組み込まれていたことを物語る貴重な証拠と考えられている。【続きを読む】 Photo: The Metal Detectives Group

金属探知機により発見された古代ローマの鉛インゴット。Photo: The Metal Detectives Group

（写真左から）ニック・ヤロープとピーター・ニコラス、土地所有者のジェライント・ジェンキンス。Photo: The Metal Detectives Group

金属探知機愛好家が「思わぬ場所」で金とガーネットの宝飾品を発見！｜2023年、イギリス東部リンカンシャー州ドニントン・オン・ベイン近郊の丘の斜面で、金属探知機愛好家が金とガーネットで作られたペンダントとブローチ計5点を発見した。この宝飾品群に関する調査結果が、このほど学術誌で発表された。【続きを読む】 Photo: The Portable Antiquities Scheme

盗難を恐れ3日間車中泊！ 金属探知機愛好家、6時間かけてローマ時代の硬貨1万5000枚を発掘｜北ウェールズで金属探知機愛好家が地中からローマ時代の硬貨1万5000枚が入った壺を探し当てた。イギリスで発見されたローマ硬貨の中では、2010年に見つかった5万2500枚に次ぐ規模となる。【続きを読む】 Photo: Facebook/Minelab Metal Detectors

金属探知機愛好家親子が畑で大発見。「子どものおもちゃ」と思った金属片が古代ローマのブローチだった！｜イギリス南部、ドーセット州ドーチェスターの畑で金属探知機愛好家親子が2000年前の青銅製ブローチを発見した。ブローチは現在、宝物認定の調査が行われている。【続きを読む】Photo: BBC Spotlight

古代ローマのブローチを見つけたマーティン・ターナー。Photo: BBC Spotlight

金属探知機愛好家が「歴史の空白」を掘り起こす！ 模造金貨のジュエリーは権力の象徴？｜イギリス・エセックス州サクステッドで金蔵探知機愛好家が中世初期のものと思われる金製のペンダントヘッドを発見した。研究者は、ローマ帝国崩壊後の同州における支配階級の存在に新たな光を投げかけるものと注目している。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy Colchester and Ipswich Museum Services

金属探知機愛好家が見つけた、中世初期のものと思われる金貨ペンダント。Photo: Courtesy Colchester and Ipswich Museum Services

8歳の少年が19世紀の難破船を発見！｜家族旅行中の8歳の男の子が誕生日プレゼントにもらった金属探知機を使ってみたところ難破船をカナダ・オンタリオ州で発見した。「湖畔で金属探知機を起動すると、『チン！』という音がし、掘ってみると大きな釘が出てきたのです」と、男の子は当時を振り返る【続きを読む】Photo: YouTube/CBC News: The National

金属探知機愛好家が申告不履行などの罪で逮捕｜イギリスで金属探知機愛好家によって発見された933枚の鉄器時代の金貨が発見された。発見者は財宝申告の不履行と窃盗の罪で逮捕された。申告を怠った発見者には報奨金が支給されず、土地の所有者のみに支払われた。なお、金貨は地元の博物館に収蔵されている。【続きを読む】Photo: Facebook/Museum of Chelmsford

畑から1400年前の純金製カラスの頭部が出土！｜金属探知機愛好家グループの新人を含む2人が2025年1月、アングロサクソン時代の金製のカラスの頭部とガーネットが埋め込まれた帯を発掘した。神話では使徒や身の前触れとして登場していたカラスだが、今回見つかった頭部が何を表現しているかはわかっていない【続きを読む】Photo: Chris Phillips

浜辺を散歩中の金属探知機愛好家が「真の芸術品」を発見！｜ポーランド・ポメラニアで、嵐の後の浜辺を探索した金属探知機愛好家が2500年前の短剣を発見。刃の根元に星に囲まれた小さな三日月のようなシンボルが、全体には星を線で繋いだ星座のような形が施されており、儀式的意義をもっていたと推測している。【続きを読む】Photo: Museum of the History of the Kamień Region

短剣の根元の拡大図。Photo: Museum of the History of the Kamień Region

イギリスで鉄器時代のお宝800点超を発見。馬具に地中海サンゴの装飾など古代史に新たな光｜イギリスのノース・ヨークシャー州メルソンビー近郊の畑で、800点を超える鉄器時代の遺物が見つかった。この種の発見としては最大規模かつ重要性が高く、イングランド北部と古代ローマの交易を示す遺物も出土している。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy Durham University

1000年前のコインに8億円超の評価額。お宝の報奨金は発見者と土地所有者に分配｜2019年、イギリス南西部で新しい金属探知機の使い方を試そうと出かけた7人のグループが、1000年前の銀のコインを大量に発見した。近頃その価値が430万ポンド（約8億4000万円）と評価され、イギリス史上最高額のお宝となった。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy of the British Museum

発見されたコインにはハロルド2世とウィリアム1世の横顔が掘られていた。後者は、1066年にウィリアム1世が戴冠した2年間に発行された。Photo: Courtesy of the British Museum

考古学の学生がバイキング時代の腕輪を発見！｜デンマーク・オーフス南部でバイキング時代に使われていた銀の腕輪が7つ出土した。考古学の学生が金属探知機を使って発見したこの腕輪によって「オーフスがバイキング時代の中心地であったことが裏付けられた」と、異物を収蔵した博物館館長は語る。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy of Moesgaard Museum

牛の頭の取っ手のある鉢や鉄器時代の桶が出土｜イギリス・ウェールズのラントリサント・バウルにある牧草地で宝探しをしていた男性が、2000年前の宝物を発見した。完全な形で出土した2点を含む8点の遺物は鉄器時代のもので、西暦1世紀後半のローマ帝国によるブリテン征服の頃に埋められた可能性が高いという。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy National Museum Wales

title_original: Yes, That’s a Wicker Penis: Inside Alexander Skarsgård’s Wild ‘Wicker’ Transformation

"https://www.indiewire.com/features/craft/avatar-fire-and-ash-costumes-james-cameron-1235176587/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "邓克利分享说，他们的目标是让这种藤条编织复制肌肉纤维；它必须足够紧密以维系整体，同时又足够宽松，以便线束能够移动和弯曲。随着藤条编织样品日臻完美，鲁巴诺透露：“这套特制服装的颈部以下有50个独立的3D打印身体部件，固定在非常薄的氨纶或强力网眼布上。然后服装的头套套过他的头部并盖过[斯卡斯加德的]下巴，这样当他移动头部时，颈部也会随之一起移动。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于面部，他们还应用了独立制作的部件：藤条耳朵、藤条嘴唇、下颌部件、更大的前额、颧骨和鼻子，鲁巴诺将其比作“蝙蝠侠面具的一部分”。此外还有假发、睫毛和面部毛发。鲁巴诺解释说，这些组件“是用新西兰亚麻植物muka制作的，这些纤维经过梳理和撕碎，然后像人类头发打在蕾丝上一样，打结编织到织物上。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/W_R_00007.jpg?w=650", "alt": "《Wicker》幕后花絮中的奥利维娅·科尔曼和亚历山大·斯卡斯加德", "caption": "《Wicker》幕后花絮 由Black Bear Pictures供图", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "维塔以其怪物和科幻生物而闻名，因此塑造一个浪漫的主角给创作者们带来了独特的挑战。邓克利强调：“我们制作的既不是人类，也不是血肉之躯的生物。”鲁巴诺补充了另一层难度：“亚历山大将被完全包裹起来，但我们需要他的神髓透射出来。”保持斯卡斯加德的相貌意味着要确保戏服具有极高的实用性：它会隐藏斯卡斯加德的皮肤，但不会隐藏他的表情。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这套戏服几乎完全是实景制作的；只有少数细节需要CGI。其中之一是阳光透过藤条丈夫编织空隙透射进来的效果。罗巴诺说：“从手肘往下，[斯卡斯加德]的前臂穿着合身的蓝色氨纶，因此VFX得以在非常关键的时刻发挥作用。唯一的其他特效是去除了泪腺、水线以及眼球周围的一点粉红色。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/W_R_00049.jpg?w=650", "alt": "《Wicker》中的奥利维娅·科尔曼和亚历山大·斯卡斯加德", "caption": "《Wicker》由Black Bear Pictures供图", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "为藤条丈夫穿衣", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管维塔创作了藤条丈夫的面部和躯干，但腰部以下的部分则需要另一双巧手。匈牙利服装设计二人组安德拉斯·丹尼尔·托特（András Dániel Tóth）和阿蒂拉·戈德纳-尤哈斯（Attila Godena-Juhász）（此前曾参与《The Uprising》和《Martin Scorsese Presents: The Saints》的工作）与邓克利和鲁巴诺紧密合作，以确保服装、轮廓和藤条假体之间的连贯性。", "links": [{"text": "The Uprising", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/the-uprising-review-1235214967/"}, {"text": "Martin Scorsese Presents: The Saints", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/interviews/francesca-martin-scorsese-interview-the-saints-1235165511/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "托特说：“在拍摄开始前一周，导演们说我们应该看看[藤条丈夫]赤身裸体的样子。”这促成了一个快速推进的戏服项目，旨在制作出无缝模仿假体的裤子。托特说：“我们发明了一种技术：在弹力底布上用特殊颜料进行打印，如果用热处理，它就是三维立体的……连藤条阴茎也包括在内，亚历克斯开玩笑说，因为他来工作室试穿了好几次，而且他真的很想知道自己的[阴茎]尺寸。这非常有意思。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随后，他们的小团队手工绘制并为每一个藤条细节阴影着色，以追求逼真感。戈德纳-尤哈斯说：“不幸的是，当他走进湖里时，这一点不是那么明显，但真的很酷。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除了柳条裤之外，托特和戈德纳-尤哈斯还负责为柳条丈夫设计服装。他们在服装上拥有相当大的自由度，不受地点或时间的限制。“如果你需要创造一个并非真实存在的村庄或宇宙，你就必须使用世人所不了解的参考元素；这就是为什么我们最终选择以匈牙利民间艺术和服饰作为灵感来源，因为在匈牙利以外，人们其实并不了解它们长什么样，”托特说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/W_R_00068.jpg?w=650", "alt": "《柳条》幕后花絮", "caption": "《柳条》幕后花絮，图片由黑熊影业提供", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除此之外，两人还指出，在为这部充满异世情色幻想的影片设计每一个服装组件之前，他们曾从17世纪、18世纪和19世纪的风格、质感和色彩中汲取灵感并制作了情绪板（moodboard）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随后便是为斯卡斯加德试穿戏服。“亚历克斯是个身材高大的男演员，当维塔工作室加上假体后，他的身材显得更魁梧了；这种轮廓实在太棒了，”托特说。“我们把他穿的每一件衣服都做得稍微小了一点，就像你在高中时穿过、后来身材长高而穿不下的衣服一样；袖口和裤脚都很短，腰围也不在正常腰部的位置。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "戈德纳-尤哈斯补充道：“另外，大家都想节省时间，不想每次都贴满全身的柳条，所以我们制作了一件加垫的内衬。这样一来，即使他只穿着衬衫、没有佩戴假体，整体的轮廓也依然保持不变。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "柳条丈夫的全面盛大亮相发生在他敲开村里各家各户的门去借衣服之后，随之而来的是一套剪裁贴身的结婚礼服，搭配一双来自匈牙利鞋匠的棕色系带鞋。“我们最终选用了一种深蓝灰色、非常高档的花呢，”托特指出。“这套三件式西装的剪裁借鉴了17世纪的男装。”这种精致的严肃感与紧身剪裁相结合，营造出一种既优雅又性感的视觉形象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/W_R_00049_283d42.jpg?w=650", "alt": "奥利维娅·科尔曼与亚历山大·斯卡斯加德在《柳条》中", "caption": "《柳条》图片由黑熊影业提供", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在随后的一场戏中，这种性感氛围得到了进一步提升：村民们震惊而又敬畏地分列两旁，注视着渔妇与柳条丈夫跳起感官热烈的情色舞蹈。“我们决定在那场戏里脱掉夹克，因为不穿夹克不仅视觉效果更高雅，也更方便他跳舞，”托特回忆道。“衬衫的剪裁相当宽松，与奥利维娅的衬衫完美呼应。真是浪漫极了。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "柳条丈夫的存在——他那郁郁寡欢的欲望，以及令整个小镇因满腔春情与妒忌而陷入狂热的奇观——正是托特、戈德纳-尤哈斯、邓克利和鲁巴诺精湛电影工艺的雄伟展示。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "谢天谢地，没有人被扎出刺。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
You’ll never look at a wicker basket the same way after “Wicker”. Based on Ursula Wills-Jones’s short story “The Wicker Husband”, the raunchy period comedy follows an outcast Fisherwoman ( Olivia Colman ) commissioning a master Basket Weaver (Peter Dinklage) to make her a wicker husband. The result is a man entirely woven of wicker whose dedication to his wife and romance is absolute; of course, it’s a role for Alexander Skarsgård .

Transforming the 6’4″ Swede into the Wicker Husband required not actual magic, but something very close to it. Art director and prosthetic makeup designer Joe Dunckley, as well as makeup and hair designer Sarah Rubano from Wētā Workshop, and their teams collaborated with directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer on creating a fully practical suit and full facial prosthetic makeup so that Skarsgård could move and emote as freely as the romance novel-inspired poster for “Wicker” promises.

“The success of the film hinged on the quality of the makeup itself; if you were going to be invested in this film, that character needed to be believable in that world,” Dunckley told IndieWire.

Over 18 months, the Wētā team researched, developed, and manufactured “Wicker”’s co-protagonist, developing an entirely new way to make prosthetic makeup in the process. “Traditional materials wouldn’t be viable because wicker’s geometry is just far too complex; it’s really unmoldable,” Dunckley said. “We had a very good understanding of the cutting edge of 3D printing technology, but we still didn’t know how exactly to do this; none of the hardware is intended to be used this way.”

Weaving the Wicker Husband

The timing was serendipitous; Wētā textiles and weaving team had just come off “ Avatar ”, where they had been weaving costumes for the Na’vi for years. Some jumped over to “Wicker” to help refine the creative process for the Wicker Husband. Explaining the creation process, Dunckley said: “Our concept team blocked out shapes, [head weaver Jasmin Van Lith] would do a physical weave sample; we’d incorporate that back into the 2D artwork. Then we’d do a 3D model of that weave, print out a test piece, and do a make-up test and see if it behaved in the way we wanted, then go back to the sampling.”

Dunckley shared that they aimed for this wicker weaving to replicate muscle fiber; it had to be tight enough to hold together but loose enough for the strands to move and flex. With the wicker weaving samples perfected, Rubano shared: “There were 50 individual 3D-printed body pieces from the neck down anchored onto very thin spandex or power mesh for the fabricated suit. Then the suit’s hood goes over his head and over [Skarsgård’s] chin so that as he moves his head, the neck moves along with him.”

For the face, they also applied individually crafted pieces: wicker ears, wicker lips, a jaw piece, a larger forehead, cheekbones, and a nose, which Rubano likens to “a Batman mask piece.” Then there’s the wig, eyelashes, and facial hair. Rubano explains these components are “made out of muka, a New Zealand flax plant, strands that are teased and shredded, and then knotted onto the weave, just like human hair onto lace.”

Wētā is famous for its monsters and sci-fi creatures, so making a romantic lead gave the creatives a unique challenge. “We weren’t making a human being or a creature of flesh and blood,” Dunckley highlighted. Rubano added the other layer of difficulty: “Alexander’s going to be completely covered up, but we need his essence to shine through.” Maintaining Skarsgård’s likeness meant ensuring the utmost practicality of the costume: it would hide Skarsgård’s skin but not his expressions.

The costume was almost entirely practical; only a few details required CGI. One of which was sunlight peeking through the woven gaps of the Wicker Husband. “From the elbows down, [Skarsgård wore] fitted blue spandex under his forearms, so VFX was possible for very key moments,” Robano said. “The only other effects were the removal of a bit of pinkness in the tear ducts, waterline and around his eyeball.”

Dressing the Wicker Husband

Though Wētā created the face and torso of the Wicker Husband, a different pair of hands was required for below the waist. Hungarian costume designer duo András Dániel Tóth and Attila Godena-Juhász (who previously worked on “ The Uprising ” and “ Martin Scorsese Presents: The Saints ”) worked closely with Dunckley and Rubano to ensure continuity with costumes, silhouettes, and the wicker prosthetics.

“One week before the shoot started, the directors said we should see [the Wicker Husband] naked,” Tóth said. That triggered a fast-tracked costume project to create pants that seamlessly mimic the prosthetics. “We invented a technique: printing on an elastic base with a special paint that, if you treat it with heat, it’s three-dimensional… wicker penis included, Alex made a joke that because he came to the workshop for several fittings, and he really wanted to know the size of his [penis]. It was a lot of fun,” Tóth said.

Their small team then hand-painted and shaded every wicker detail for realism. “Unfortunately, it’s not so visible when he’s walking into the lake, but it was very cool,” Godena-Juhász said.

Beyond the wicker pants, Tóth and Godena-Juhász also dressed the Wicker Husband. They were granted freedom with costumes, not restricted by place or time. “If you need to create a village, a universe that [doesn’t really exist], you need to use references that aren’t known to the world; that’s why we ended up using Hungarian folk art and garments as an inspiration, because outside of Hungary, no one really knows what it looks like,” Tóth said.

Alongside this, the pair note that they also moodboarded inspiration from 17th-, 18th-, and 19th-century styles, textures, and colours before designing every costume component of this otherworldly erotic fantasy.

Then came time to get Skarsgård kitted up. “Alex is a big guy, and [when] Wētā added the prosthetics, they made him even bigger; it was such a nice silhouette,” Tóth said. “We made every piece of garment he’s wearing a little bit smaller, like it’s the suit you wore in high school and grew out of; the sleeves and hemline of the pants are short, and the waistline is not at the waist.”

Godena-Juhász added: “Also, everybody wanted to save time, and not apply the whole [wicker] body, so we made a padded under-layer. So even if he’s wearing the shirt, without the prosthetics, the silhouette remains the same.”

The Wicker Husband’s full-scale grand reveal comes after he knocks on doors around the village to borrow clothes, resulting in a snug-fitting wedding suit paired with brown laced shoes from a Hungarian shoemaker. “We ended up using this dark blue-greyish, very fancy tweed,” Tóth noted. “The cut of the three-piece suit is referring to the 17th-century menswear.” That refined seriousness, paired with the skin-tight fit, creates an image of both sophistication and sexiness.

The latter is elevated in a later scene where the villager crowd parts, in shock and awe, to watch the Fisherwoman and Wicker Husband’s sensual dancing. “We decided to lose the jacket for that scene because it’s far more elevated and easier for him to dance without the jacket,” Tóth recalled. “The cut of the shirt was quite oversized, matching perfectly with Olivia’s blouse. It’s so romantic.”

The Wicker Husband’s presence — his brooding desire, and the spectacle driving the whole town wild with horny jealousy — is a majestic demonstration of cinematic craft from Tóth and Godena-Juhász and Dunckley and Rubano.

Thankfully, no one got splinters.
excerpt_original: And yes, those are also wicker nipples.

article_text:
Torna il 18 novembre, a Milano, l’ Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Pandolfini . Un appuntamento con un catalogo particolarmente ampio, che riunisce opere provenienti da prestigiose collezioni private, alcune delle quali inedite sul mercato, e attraversa alcune delle stagioni più significative dell’arte del Novecento, con uno sguardo aperto anche alla ricerca contemporanea. C’è tutto quello che ha reso il secolo scorso uno dei periodi più interessanti per il collezionismo: dal surrealismo di Salvador Dalí alla materia di Lucio Fontana; arrivando al presente, fino a un’opera di Giulia Cenci, tra le artiste italiane più riconosciute nel panorama internazionale, la cui ricerca è stata protagonista anche della 59ª Biennale di Venezia del 2022, Il latte dei sogni . Le provenienze aggiungono un ulteriore livello di interesse alla selezione, come nel caso del Crocifisso in terracotta dipinta di Lucio Fontana, acquistato direttamente dall’artista dall’attuale collezionista presso la fornace di Albisola Marina, o del lavoro su carta di Jannis Kounellis, proveniente dalla storica Galleria La Tartaruga.

Sguardo agli highlights di Pandolfini, dal Novecento al presente

Tra i protagonisti dell’incanto figura Salvador Dalí, presente con Senza titolo [Don Chisciotte vedendo che il suo avversario non attaccava, si arrestò a metà della sua corsa] , opera appartenente al ciclo dedicato alle avventure del celebre cavaliere della Mancia, proposta con una stima di 50.000-100.000 euro. Un soggetto che trova un interessante contrappunto in Combattimento tra due cavalieri di Giorgio de Chirico, valutato 18.000-30.000 euro: due interpretazioni differenti, ma accomunate dalla centralità dell’immaginario cavalleresco.

Sul versante delle esperienze che hanno ridefinito il rapporto tra arte e spazio, si segnala Running Fence (Project for Sonoma and Marin Counties, State of California) di Christo, con una stima di 60.000-80.000 euro. Il lavoro rimanda alla dimensione monumentale dei progetti ambientali realizzati da Christo insieme a Jeanne-Claude a partire dagli anni Sessanta – una ricerca che ha progressivamente esteso i confini dell’intervento artistico, portandolo fuori dai luoghi tradizionali dell’esposizione.

Tra i top lot anche Alighiero Boetti, in catalogo con due opere che restituiscono la complessità del suo metodo e il suo interesse per i sistemi di classificazione, la serialità e il rapporto tra ordine e casualità. Da una parte 1000 shoots one 0 , stimato 30.000-50.000 euro; dall’altra un raro esemplare del libro con copertina ricamata Classifying the thousand longest rivers in the world , in catalogo a 20.000-30.000 euro.

Giacomo Balla è offerto da Pandolfini con opere che permettono di attraversare differenti momenti della sua vicenda artistica, dagli esordi ritrattistici fino alla stagione futurista. A quest’ultima appartengono Paesaggio futurista , stimato 30.000-50.000 euro, e Linee di velocità + spazio , valutato 20.000-30.000 euro, entrambi realizzati tra il 1915 e il 1920. Per Casorati è stata selezionata una serie di ritratti che attraversa oltre trent’anni della sua produzione, dagli anni Venti agli anni Cinquanta. Di Guttuso spicca invece Omaggio a Van Gogh (Corvi su campo di grano) , olio su tela del 1966, stimato 18.000-30.000 euro e già appartenuto alla collezione di Lino Mezzacane.

La stagione futurista è ulteriormente approfondita attraverso opere di Fortunato Depero, Enrico Prampolini, Mina Loy e Roberto Marcello Baldessari. Di quest’ultimo viene proposta La Vraie Italie , con una stima di 30.000-50.000 euro, lavoro riconducibile a una delle fasi più interessanti della sua produzione. Si prosegue con Salvo , rappresentato da due opere Senza titolo , rispettivamente del 1984 e del 1995, con stime di 45.000-80.000 e 35.000-60.000 euro. Accanto a lui, Mario Schifano , con una selezione di lavori che attraversa diverse fasi della sua produzione dagli anni Settanta agli anni Novanta, e Franco Angeli, autore di Icona primo viaggio attraverso le emozioni di un paese chiamato URSS insieme a Marina, con Marina, a Marina , realizzata tra il 1971 e il 1972 e stimata 20.000-30.000 euro.

Non manca poi uno sguardo sulle evoluzioni della pittura italiana, con opere di Afro, Giorgio Griffa e Mario Nigro, fino alla Transavanguardia, rappresentata da Sandro Chia e Mimmo Paladino. Di quest’ultimo sono presenti una scultura in bronzo e una gouache su cartoncino del 1982. Completa il nucleo Luigi Ontani, figura tra le più originali della scena artistica italiana dagli anni Settanta, con la monumentale maschera Prim , realizzata negli anni Novanta e stimata 30.000-50.000 euro, oltre a due acquerelli su carta. E ancora Igor Mitoraj , in catalogo con Testa di Madonna (50.000-90.000 euro) e Decurione (20.000-30.000 euro).

Lo sguardo si estende fino al presente: in ambito contemporaneo, Pandolfini presenta nomi come Shirin Neshat, Rebecca Horn, Bertozzi & Casoni e Jago. Menzione importante, per l’opera di Giulia Cenci dal titolo Pissing female dog , del 2019.
